claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced by conventional powder methods without dispersoid additions.
Adding approximately 0.5 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles during synthesis will produce a uniform oxide dispersion.
A 0.5 wt% Y2O3 dispersion will suppress radiation-induced precipitation in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening.
The Y2O3 addition will improve the alloy's suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Irradiation at 600–800°C is relevant to fusion service.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will stabilize grain boundaries.
Y2O3 particles will provide preferential sites for recombination or annihilation of irradiation-induced point defects.
The oxide dispersion will reduce the concentration of free irradiation-induced defects.
Reducing the free-defect concentration will diminish the driving force for radiation-induced precipitation.
The defect-sink action of Y2O3 will not adversely affect alloy hardness.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have a significantly lower radiation-induced precipitate number density than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have smaller radiation-induced precipitates than the unmodified alloy.
Irradiation hardening in the Y2O3-modified alloy will remain below approximately a 10% increase.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops notable precipitation under approximately 8 dpa irradiation.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 shows only negligible hardness changes under approximately 8 dpa irradiation.
The proposed effect is applicable up to approximately 8 dpa between 600°C and 800°C and may deviate outside those boundaries.
